etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English axen, aksen, axien, from Old English ācsian and āxian, showing metathesis from āscian. Ax/aks was common in literary works until about 1600.

definitions.definition: (now nonstandard or dialectical, especially African-American Vernacular, MLE and Bermuda) Alternative form of ask

quote.citation: 1526, [William Tyndale, transl.], The Newe Testamẽt […] (Tyndale Bible), [Worms, Germany: Peter Schöffer], →OCLC, Acts:
quote.text: When they were come togedder, they axed off hym, sayinge: Master wilt thou at this tyme restore agayne the kyngdom of israhel?

quote.citation: 1836, Joanna Baillie, The Alienated Manor, act 4:
quote.text: Dolly: And if so be, why did you ax me to keep you company? Housekeeper wants me below to pick raisins.

quote.citation: 1879, William Barnes, “The Welshnut Tree”, in Complete Poems, volume 1, page 106:
quote.text: Ar try who'l ax em the hardest riddle,Ar soonest vind out oone put us, true...
Richard Dauntless: "But, axin' your pardon, miss, might I be permitted to salute the flag I'm a-goin' to sail under?"

quote.citation: 1979, Verna Mae Slone, What My Heart Wants to Tell, page 18:
quote.text: ‘I axed him if he knowed the way and he said he had not fergitten the lay of the land.’

quote.citation: 2006 Sept. 17, David Mills, "Soft Eyes", The Wire, 00:19:01:
quote.text: Wise: Your boy left here a while agoJohnson: I ain' lookin' for him. He at his granmother's. I wanted to ax you somethin'.

quote.citation: 2013 September 5, James Burton, The Bermuda Sun‎[1], archived from the original on 12 December 2022:
quote.text: He's cool. Does triathlons dahn de Sahn. Don't drink. Ax me if I want a lift to de beach — he hurd it's a dahnce goin on dahn thurr.
